title: the door of the guru
hook: the door of the guru; why it's open to anyone
carry: cover your head, take off your shoes, come in

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangat, the company you keep. Your line was good company. Who did you tell? Day fourteen, the end of week two.

You're walking down a street you know, and you notice a tall triangular flag, saffron or deep blue, flying on a pole outside a building you never paid much attention to. Maybe it's a grand white building with domes. Maybe it's a converted warehouse, or an old church, or a house. Through the door you can hear singing, and drums, and smell something cooking. You might wonder: can I just walk in? Am I allowed? Do I have to be one of them? This week you've learned the kitchen, the pillars, the turban and the company. Today, the place where they all meet, and the answer to that question.
screen: `A TALL FLAG ON A POLE.` → `SINGING, DRUMS, SOMETHING COOKING.` → `CAN I JUST WALK IN?`

segments.voice: Gurdwara. Gur, the Guru. Dwara, a door, a gateway. The door of the Guru. It's the Sikh place of worship, and the flag outside, the Nishan Sahib, is there so it can be found from far away. And the answer to the question is yes. Anyone can walk in, of any faith or none. The most famous gurdwara, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, was built with doors on all four sides, which Sikhs explain as a welcome to people from every direction and every walk of life. There are just a few simple things everyone does, Sikh or not. Cover your head, with a scarf or a cloth, and gurdwaras usually keep some at the door. Take off your shoes. Wash your hands. Leave tobacco and alcohol outside. That's all. Inside, you'll find the week's words gathered in one place. At the front, on a raised platform under a canopy, rests the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib. People come in, bow before it, and sit on the floor, all at the same level. That's the sangat. Musicians sing hymns from the scripture: that's naam japna, out loud. Near the end, everyone may be offered karah prashad, a warm sweet made of flour, butter and sugar, placed in cupped hands, the same for everyone. Then, down the hall, the langar: the one row, the same meal. And the people cooking it, cleaning the floors, minding the shoes? That's seva, and every coin that keeps the lights on is someone's vand chakna. A gurdwara isn't only a place to pray. It's the whole path, given a building and a door that stays open.
screen: `GUR, THE GURU. DWARA, A DOOR.` · `OPEN TO ANYONE, FROM EVERY SIDE.` · `HEAD COVERED, SHOES OFF, HANDS WASHED.` · `THE WHOLE WEEK UNDER ONE ROOF.` · then, large: `A DOOR THAT STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself at the door of a gurdwara. You slip off your shoes. You tie a cloth over your head. You rinse your hands in cool water. You step inside, onto soft carpet, and sit on the floor among strangers while someone sings. Nobody asks who you are. Just sit there in your mind and listen. The bell holds the time.
The gurdwara. The door of the Guru, the Sikh place of worship, open to anyone. Fourteenth word. Two weeks.

Your line: cover your head, take off your shoes, come in. Look up the nearest gurdwara to you today, just to know it's there. Next week, the last of camp one: spirit, story, prayer and the book itself. Day fourteen.

howItsDone: Anyone may visit a gurdwara: visitors cover their heads, remove their shoes and wash their hands, sit on the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib for kirtan, receive karah prashad, and eat in the langar.

fork.reveal: anyone may come in. head covered, shoes off, hands washed, and a seat on the floor with everyone else.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: gur (the Guru) + duara (door): the door of the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh temple.
what it means: the door of the Guru, where the scripture rests and the congregation, the kitchen and the service all meet, open to anyone.
what a scholar hears: early Sikh gathering places were called dharamsals. the name gurdwara, the Guru's door, took hold later, and the Nishan Sahib marks one from a distance.
